title: Control Interfaces & Operations
contentStatus: REVISED per Content Principles (60% pass, technical terminology + explanatory notes). Dashboard/status light specifics still pending SME confirmation.

sections.title: Meeting the Human-Machine Interface
learningObjectives: Understand what the ANT interface is and who uses it
Recognize the difference between monitoring MoRo and actively controlling it
sections.content: Every MoRo unit is managed through a Human-Machine Interface (HMI) — software that lets an operator see and direct what the machine is doing, rather than controlling it through physical switches alone. MoRo's HMI is called ANT. You don't need a technical background to use it. Most day-to-day interaction is supervisory: you observe operations, confirm actions, and intervene only when needed — not continuous hands-on control.

keyTerms.note: The software layer through which an operator interacts with and monitors a machine's operations.
MoRo's HMI platform, used for fleet monitoring and mission control.
Overseeing an automated system's operation without directly performing each action yourself.

sections.title: Reading the Dashboard
learningObjectives: Identify the main categories of information on the dashboard
Know where to find MoRo's current status versus its assigned tasks
sections.content: The ANT dashboard organizes information around three operational questions: MoRo's current location and state (fleet status), what it's currently assigned to do (mission status), and configuration options (system settings). The exact menu structure and terminology within ANT will be confirmed against the live system before this section is finalized — the operational logic described here holds regardless of the final interface layout.

keyTerms.note: A real-time view of where each MoRo unit is and what state it's in.
The current and queued tasks assigned to a unit.

sections.title: Startup Sequence
learningObjectives: List the sequence of checks before powering on MoRo
Understand why a system-ready confirmation matters before assigning work
sections.content: Startup follows a defined sequence, not a single action. Before power-on, conduct a visual check to confirm the intended path is clear and sensors are unobstructed. On power-on, MoRo runs an internal diagnostic — verifying battery charge, navigation calibration, and safety system function — before reporting a ready state. Operators must wait for this ready confirmation before assigning a mission; assigning work before diagnostics complete is a common, avoidable cause of interrupted starts.

keyTerms.note: MoRo's automatic self-check of its systems (battery, navigation, safety) run at startup.
The confirmed status indicating MoRo has passed its startup diagnostic and can accept mission assignments.

sections.title: Manual Override & Emergency Stop
learningObjectives: Understand when manual override is appropriate versus autonomous operation
Know how emergency stop functions relative to manual and autonomous modes
sections.content: MoRo operates autonomously by default. Manual override exists for specific situations — repositioning during setup, clearing a blocked path, or post-maintenance testing. Manual override does not disable safety systems. Emergency stop (E-stop) functions identically in both manual and autonomous modes: it takes immediate priority and halts all operation regardless of current state.

keyTerms.note: Operator-initiated direct control of MoRo, used for specific non-routine situations.
MoRo's default operating state, in which it executes missions independently.
An immediate, unconditional halt command that overrides all other operation.

sections.title: Mission Lifecycle
learningObjectives: Describe the basic mission lifecycle: load, start, monitor, pause, resume
Understand what happens to a paused mission
sections.content: A mission moves through a defined lifecycle: it's loaded, started, monitored during execution, and can be paused or resumed as needed. Pausing a mission is not the same as cancelling it — MoRo holds position safely and resumes from the same point once cleared. Understanding this lifecycle is the operational foundation for everything covered in L2.

sections.title: Status Indicators
learningObjectives: Recognize what MoRo's status indicators communicate at a glance
Distinguish between routine status signals and signals requiring attention
sections.content: Beyond the dashboard, MoRo communicates status directly through visual indicators — useful for floor-level awareness without checking a screen. These fall into general categories: normal operation, waiting/paused, and attention-needed. The confirmed color-and-pattern reference will be added once verified against current MoRo hardware documentation.

keyTerms.note: A visual signal (light) on the MoRo unit itself that communicates its current operating state.

questions.question: What is the ANT interface (HMI)?
options: The software through which operators monitor and control MoRo
questions.feedback: Correct. ANT is MoRo's Human-Machine Interface — the software layer for monitoring and control.

questions.question: What must be confirmed before assigning a mission?
options: Nothing — missions can be assigned immediately
That MoRo has completed its internal diagnostic and reached ready state
questions.feedback: Correct. A ready state confirmation, following the internal diagnostic, is required before mission assignment.

questions.question: Does E-stop behave differently in manual override versus autonomous mode?
options: Yes, manual mode uses a separate procedure
E-stop only functions in autonomous mode
No — E-stop takes immediate priority identically in both modes

questions.question: What happens when a mission is paused rather than cancelled?
options: MoRo returns to its charging dock automatically
MoRo holds position safely and resumes from the same point
questions.feedback: Correct. Pausing preserves mission state; cancelling does not.

questions.question: What is the purpose of MoRo's status indicators?
options: To communicate operating state at a glance, without checking a screen
To replace the need for the dashboard entirely
To show the time of day
questions.feedback: Correct. Status indicators provide floor-level visibility independent of the dashboard.
